candidates.name: The Claim You Deserve: Denied & Underpaid Home Insurance Claim Corpus
candidates.one_line: A 50-state reference corpus (unfair-claims-practices deadlines, appraisal-clause rules, roof/siding matching regulations, DOI complaint procedures, sample demand letters) that turns the buyer's own ChatGPT/Claude into a competent analyst of their denial letter and policy.
candidates.buyer: Individual US homeowner whose wind/hail/water/fire claim was denied or underpaid, facing a $10k-80k repair; already googling at midnight, already has or will open ChatGPT in the next ten minutes because every news story now tells them AI beats insurers. Consumer, not business.
candidates.the_expensive_moment: The denial or lowball letter arrives after a storm. The roofer wants $28k, the insurer offered $9k or nothing, the public adjuster wants 10-20% and the lawyer wants 33-40% contingency. The homeowner has a suit-limitation clock running they usually don't know about.
candidates.money_at_stake: Average claim severity: wind/hail $14,747 (2019-2023), water damage/freezing ~$15,400, fire $84k+ (III-derived figures reported across ConsumerAffairs/MoneyGeek stat pages, search-verified [PLAUSIBLE]; I did not fetch iii.org directly). A public adjuster's 10-20% on a $30k dispute is $3,000-6,000 — the folder at $167 is 3-5% of that.
candidates.whats_in_the_folder: instructions.md (how to feed your denial letter + policy to the AI, with hard guardrails: information only); /statutes: 50-state unfair-claims-settlement-practices acts as normalized markdown with acknowledgment/decision/payment deadlines and exact citations; /matching: the ~30 state matching/line-of-sight bulletins and regulations for roof-siding disputes (e.g., state bulletins that force full-slope or full-roof replacement), dated and cited; /appraisal: appraisal-clause law state by state (who can invoke, binding or not, umpire procedure, cost-shifting), incl. new legislation like Colorado HB26-1247; /deadlines: suit-limitation periods and proof-of-loss requirements by state; /complaints: all 50 DOI complaint portals, forms and what each DOI actually does; /samples: appraisal demand letters, DOI complaints, document-request letters, a worked before/after estimate dispute; /glossary: Xactimate line-item and depreciation concepts the adjuster will use.
candidates.source_count: 120-150 distinct sources: 50 state statutes/regs, ~50 DOI websites and bulletin archives, ~30 matching bulletins/regulatory notices, NAIC model acts, plus sample-document construction. Nobody has published this as one machine-readable set.
candidates.assembly_effort: 3-4 weeks of Claude-Code-assisted scraping, normalizing and dating, which is exactly Sol's strength. NOT rebuildable in an afternoon: any single state is an afternoon; the value is 50 states normalized, cited and dated, plus the matching-bulletin layer, which is genuinely obscure (buried DOI bulletin PDFs).
candidates.what_ai_gets_wrong_without_it: Exact statute citations and insurer response deadlines (models invent section numbers), and above all state matching rules — whether Ohio/Kentucky/Florida requires replacing the whole roof slope when shingles are discontinued is bulletin-level knowledge models reliably fuzz or hallucinate. Hallucinated citations in a demand letter destroy the homeowner's credibility with the insurer. Untested directly this session [PLAUSIBLE], but this class of citation-hallucination is well established.
candidates.prompt_test: Best buyer prompt: 'Here is my denial letter and policy. What are my rights in Texas, what deadlines apply, and draft an appraisal demand.' A good model captures maybe 40%: it explains appraisal and bad faith generically, but it cannot reliably produce the correct Texas Prompt Payment of Claims deadlines with citations, the current matching bulletin, or the DOI complaint mechanics — and it will make some of them up confidently.
candidates.volume_math: $167 x 48 sales/month = $8,016. Pool: tens of millions of homeowner claims per year, with wind/hail alone 41% of losses; even 1 purchase per ~10,000 denied/disputed claims clears the target. Storm seasons create demand spikes. Support load at ~48 units/month is manageable for one person with a good FAQ.
candidates.channel: Organic search on the buyer's words ('roof claim denied what to do', 'insurance lowballed my water damage claim', 'appraisal clause [state]') via a content site with free state-summary pages funneling to the paid corpus; plus Gumroad marketplace listing; plus non-spam participation impossible for her — instead answer-page SEO where Reddit/insurance threads rank. Paid ads viable at $167 if organic proves out.
candidates.demand_evidence: Search-verified: dozens of law-firm and roofer content pages exist precisely because the query volume exists ('Roof Damage Claim Denied? Here's How You Respond' hermanwells.com; claimback.app/blog/water-damage-claim-denied; metrocityroofing appraisal-101 page) [VERIFIED as fetched search results, HTTP 200 via search]. Colorado just legislated mandatory appraisal (HB26-1247, leg.colorado.gov) showing the dispute volume is a policy issue. One cited stat: '60% of appealed water damage denials are overturned' (lawrencelaws.com) [PLAUSIBLE].
candidates.free_substitute_check: United Policyholders (uphelp.org) — I fetched their Claim Guidance Library, HTTP 200: extensive free guidance on fire/water/hail claims, sample letters (policy request, ALE extension, mortgage release), 'Insurance Appraisal Simplified', and some state-specific pages (CA, TX, AL, TN) [VERIFIED]. This is the closest competitor and it is genuinely good — but it is coaching prose for humans, not a normalized 50-state statute/deadline/matching corpus an AI can apply to a specific denial letter, its sample letters do not cover appraisal demands with state citations, and its state coverage is partial. State DOIs each publish their own guidance (scattered — which is the product). Public adjusters and contingency lawyers are paid substitutes at 10-40%.
candidates.saturation_check: No home-insurance AI pack found. ClaimBack (claimback.app) fetched, HTTP 200: free AI appeal letters but 'designed for medical/health insurance only', no home coverage [VERIFIED]. Etsy has a generic 'Property Tax Appeal Letter Template' style of Word letters but banned AI prompt bundles in July 2024 [PLAUSIBLE]. Searches for etsy/gumroad 'insurance claim appeal AI pack' returned only health-insurance tools and generic prompt bundles — no incumbent in home-property claims [VERIFIED as a negative search result, which is weaker evidence].
candidates.regulated_check: Adjacent professions: public adjusting (licensed in most states) and law. The line: the folder supplies published statutes, deadlines, procedures and sample document formats — classic self-help publishing (the Nolo line). Permitted copy: 'This folder contains every state's insurer response deadlines and matching bulletins, with citations, so your AI can check them against your denial letter.' Forbidden copy: 'We'll tell you if your denial was wrongful' / 'We negotiate your claim' / any per-buyer review. Sol never sees a buyer's claim (H6), never values a loss, never advises invoking appraisal in a specific case — the buyer's own AI does the applying.
candidates.piracy_answer: Buyers are one-shot and desperate; they don't congregate in a persistent community after resolution the way UGC creators do. Main limits: quarterly dated updates (DOI bulletins, statutes and the appraisal-law landscape change — Colorado's 2027 law is proof), per-buyer invisible watermarking of the files, and a corpus of 100+ files that is awkward to repost. Residual risk accepted: a copy will eventually hit a subreddit; stale-dated copies of deadline-critical material are self-discrediting.
candidates.weakest_link: United Policyholders is close enough that the sales page must win on 'machine-readable, cited, all 50 states, works with your AI' — if UP ever publishes a structured dataset, the moat thins. Second: money-at-stake averages are from III-derived aggregator pages, not fetched from iii.org directly.
candidates.evidence: [VERIFIED] uphelp.org/claim-guidance-publications/ fetched HTTP 200 (free library scope as described). [VERIFIED] claimback.app fetched HTTP 200 (medical-only, free for individuals). [VERIFIED] counterforcehealth.org fetched HTTP 200 (health-denial niche is served free — kills the founder's original health angle, does not touch property). [VERIFIED] appealdesk.com fetched HTTP 200 ($49 flat done-for-you property-tax packet — killed the property-tax candidate). [VERIFIED-negative] no home-claims AI pack surfaced in targeted Gumroad/Etsy searches.

candidates.name: Seized at the Border: the CBP Cash & Goods Seizure Response Corpus
candidates.one_line: The complete assembled body of CBP seizure-response reference material — 19 CFR Part 171 with the published mitigation guidelines, CAFRA deadlines, the election-of-proceedings mechanics, port FP&F directory, and annotated sample petitions — so the buyer's own AI can walk them through responding to a Notice of Seizure without a $4,000 lawyer.
candidates.buyer: Individual traveler whose $10k-90k in cash was seized at a US airport or land border for a FinCEN-105 reporting violation (often immigrant families carrying savings — many are more comfortable in a second language, which their own AI handles); secondary tier: small e-commerce importers with detained/seized merchandise. Both are desperate, deadline-bound, and will paste a scanned notice into ChatGPT within minutes.
candidates.the_expensive_moment: CBP walks them to a back room, counts and takes every dollar, and hands them Form 6051S. Weeks later a certified-mail Notice of Seizure arrives with an Election of Proceedings form and a hard 30-35 day CAFRA clock. Attorneys quote $3,500-5,000 flat or ~30% contingency. They are searching 'CBP seized my money at airport' that same night.
candidates.money_at_stake: CBP seized an average of $152,418/day in FY2024 (~$55.6M/year) and $182,465/day in FY2025 — cbp.gov enforcement statistics pages [VERIFIED via search results quoting cbp.gov/newsroom/stats]. Individual seizures in CBP's own press releases run $21k-$190k per traveler group (Dulles, Philadelphia releases, cbp.gov) [VERIFIED]. Typical single-traveler seizure ~$8-15k [PLAUSIBLE].
candidates.whats_in_the_folder: instructions.md (feed your Notice of Seizure to your AI; hard information-only guardrails); /law: 19 CFR Part 171 normalized, 18 USC 983 (CAFRA) timeline tables, 31 USC 5316/5317 reporting offenses; /mitigation: CBP's published mitigation guidelines for currency reporting violations — the remission percentage bands by violation type and aggravating/mitigating factors, the single most hallucinated fact in this domain; /process: the Election of Proceedings form decoded option by option with the statutory consequence of each (petition vs. offer vs. CAFRA claim), decision timelines, what happens past $100k (HQ decides); /ports: FP&F office contact directory for major ports, assembled from ~40 scattered cbp.gov pages; /evidence: the legitimate-source and legitimate-use documentation checklists (bank records, payroll, sale documents, affidavit formats); /samples: annotated skeleton petitions (Form 4609/4630) and a verified-claim format; /importers: seizure/detention track for merchandise incl. ICP052 'Seizures' and liquidated-damages mitigation tables.
candidates.source_count: 60-80 distinct sources: CFR sections and appendices, two USC titles, CBP forms 4609/4630/6051S with instructions, FinCEN 105, CBP Informed Compliance Publications, the mitigation-guidelines documents, ~40 port FP&F pages, DOJ Asset Forfeiture Policy Manual excerpts, and case-outcome write-ups for the annotated samples.
candidates.assembly_effort: 3-4 weeks: the mitigation guidelines and FP&F directory are the slow, genuinely scattered part (buried PDFs and per-port pages). Not an afternoon rebuild: a chat model can summarize CAFRA generically in an afternoon but cannot reproduce the mitigation percentage tables or the port directory without inventing them.
candidates.what_ai_gets_wrong_without_it: The mitigation/remission percentage bands (models confidently invent numbers), the exact interplay of the 35-day CAFRA claim deadline vs. petition tolling, what each Election of Proceedings checkbox legally forfeits, and port-specific filing addresses. In a domain where a missed checkbox or deadline forfeits five figures permanently, hallucination is catastrophic — which is the sales pitch.
candidates.prompt_test: Best buyer prompt: 'CBP seized $18,000 from me at JFK for not reporting, here is the notice — what are my options and deadlines?' A good model captures ~50%: solid on the general CAFRA framework and honest-source narrative, but it will guess the remission percentages, blur petition-vs-claim consequences, and cannot supply the FP&F specifics or a properly structured petition skeleton. The dangerous half is exactly what it fakes.
candidates.volume_math: $297 x 26 sales/month = $7,722. Estimated case volume: ~$55.6M/yr seized ÷ ~$9-12k average seizure ≈ 4,500-6,000 currency cases/yr ≈ 400-500/month [PLAUSIBLE arithmetic on verified totals], plus merchandise seizures/detentions on top. Needing ~5% of monthly cases is aggressive — this is honestly the thin spot, mitigated by the importer tier and by price headroom (a $397 importer edition). At 26 units/month support load is trivial.
candidates.channel: Organic search on desperate exact-match queries ('CBP seized my cash at airport', 'notice of seizure election of proceedings what to choose', 'petition for remission CBP') — searchers are highly motivated and law-firm pages currently monopolize results with lead-gen content that withholds the actual tables; a content site with genuinely complete free explainer pages funneling to the corpus can rank on long-tail. Gumroad as secondary. No audience, no calls, consistent with faceless.
candidates.demand_evidence: The query space is saturated with law-firm lead-gen precisely because desperate search volume exists: greatlakescustomslaw.com maintains an entire money-seizures content hub (election-of-proceedings page, 'A Perfect Petition Is Critical' page) claiming '$11M+ recovered, 700+ cases' [VERIFIED fetch of greatlakescustomslaw.com/customs-money-seizure/, HTTP 200]; Tampa and San Diego defense firms run dedicated airport-cash-seizure practices with flat-fee/contingency offers [VERIFIED as search results]. CBP's own press releases document a steady drumbeat of multi-traveler seizures at Dulles alone [VERIFIED cbp.gov].
candidates.free_substitute_check: Named: (1) CBP itself — Forms 4609/4630 with instructions and ICP052 'Seizures' PDF are free on cbp.gov [VERIFIED via search]; they tell you the form exists, not the mitigation math or strategy landscape. (2) Great Lakes Customs Law's free blog/video series — the best free material, but structured as lead-gen: it explains concepts and then argues you need the firm ('A Perfect Petition Is Critical') [VERIFIED fetch]. (3) Institute for Justice publishes forfeiture advocacy, not case-response corpora [PLAUSIBLE]. No nonprofit assembles the mitigation guidelines + port directory + annotated samples as a usable set.
candidates.saturation_check: Zero AI packs, GPT products or DIY kits found: targeted searches for 'customs seizure / CAFRA petition template kit gumroad etsy' returned only CBP's own forms, law-firm pages, and unrelated Etsy 'gumroad template' party-favor listings [VERIFIED-negative search]. The niche's incumbents are $3,500-5,000 lawyers, not products.
candidates.regulated_check: Adjacent: law (asset forfeiture) and customs brokerage (19 CFR 111 'customs business'). Filing one's own petition pro se is expressly permitted (CBP's own form instructions address petitioners directly). The line: the folder supplies the published regulations, deadline tables, mitigation guidelines, evidence checklists and annotated formats — information. Permitted copy: 'Contains CBP's published mitigation guidelines and every deadline, so your AI can explain your notice to you.' Forbidden: 'We'll tell you whether to petition or file a claim' / any review of a buyer's notice / any filing on anyone's behalf. The petition-vs-CAFRA-claim strategy split (which firms market hard) is presented as both statutory tracks with published consequences, never a per-buyer recommendation.
candidates.piracy_answer: The buyer pool is transient one-shot individuals in a crisis; there is no persistent community of past victims to share into (unlike hobby niches). Limits: per-buyer watermarking, quarterly dated updates (port FP&F contacts and guideline revisions go stale, and the cover page says so), and the fact that a pirated stale copy with a wrong deadline is worse than nothing. Accepted residual risk is low here — this is the format's best-case piracy profile.
candidates.weakest_link: Volume: ~26 sales/month may be 5%+ of all monthly currency-seizure cases, which is a big share for a new site to capture against entrenched law-firm SEO; the importer merchandise tier and price headroom are the hedge. Second: some buyers face parallel criminal exposure (structuring), where any product must loudly say 'lawyer, now' — that page must exist and be unmissable.
candidates.evidence: [VERIFIED] cbp.gov/newsroom/stats/cbp-enforcement-statistics-fy2024 & fy2025 (via search result quotes): $152,418/day FY2024, $182,465/day FY2025 seized. [VERIFIED] greatlakescustomslaw.com/customs-money-seizure/ fetched HTTP 200: free video guide series, '$11M+ recovered, 700+ cases', no published fees. [VERIFIED] cbp.gov Form 4609 and Form 4630 pages exist (search results, cbp.gov URLs). [VERIFIED] cbp.gov Dulles/Philadelphia press releases: individual seizures $21k-$190k. [VERIFIED-negative] no DIY kit/AI pack in targeted marketplace searches. [PLAUSIBLE] attorney flat fees $3,500-5,000 and contingency structures (nationalsecuritylawfirm.com, sandiegodefenders.com search results). [PLAUSIBLE] average seizure size ~$9-12k (arithmetic, not a fetched per-case statistic; cbp.gov stats dashboard returned HTTP 403 to direct fetch).

candidates.name: Office Action Answer Kit — the assembled record of trademark refusal responses that actually won
candidates.one_line: A corpus of real, successful USPTO office action responses pulled from public TSDR records, organized by refusal type with verified citations, so a self-filer's own ChatGPT/Claude can draft a response to their 2(d) or descriptiveness refusal instead of paying an attorney $500-2,000.
candidates.buyer: A US-domiciled small-business owner (e-commerce brand, Etsy/Shopify seller, startup founder) who self-filed a trademark application for $250-350/class and just received a substantive office action. An individual acting for their business. Note the boundary: foreign-domiciled applicants MUST be represented by a US attorney per USPTO rule, so the market is US self-filers only [PLAUSIBLE, well-established USPTO domicile rule, not fetched this session]. This buyer self-filed precisely because they are DIY and cost-sensitive, and in 2026 they are overwhelmingly already using ChatGPT — H8 satisfied.
candidates.the_expensive_moment: The office action email arrives. They have a hard 3-month statutory deadline to respond (extension available for a fee) or the application is ABANDONED and the filing fee is lost [VERIFIED — uspto.gov/trademarks/maintain/responding-office-actions, fetched HTTP 200: 'within three months from the date it issued']. Autocomplete confirms people search 'trademark office action response extension fee' — they are counting days.
candidates.money_at_stake: Filing fees already sunk ($250-350/class) plus the attorney alternative: Trademark Engine's attorney-assisted office action response 'starts at $599' [VERIFIED — trademarkengine.com/office-action-response/, fetched HTTP 200]. Secondary sources put typical attorney flat fees at $500-2,000, with recent claims of $1,500-3,500 [PLAUSIBLE — michaelmeyerlaw.com, kicksaaslegal.com, upcounsel.com via search]. Plus the brand itself: losing the mark can mean an Amazon Brand Registry rejection and a rebrand.
candidates.whats_in_the_folder: (1) INSTRUCTIONS.md — how to feed the buyer's own office action PDF to their AI and have it drafted against the corpus, with the information/advice disclaimer baked in. (2) /winning-responses/ — 150-300 real applicant responses retrieved from TSDR public records, filtered to applications that received a refusal and subsequently REGISTERED, organized as 2d-likelihood-of-confusion/, 2e1-descriptiveness/, specimen-refusals/, identification-amendments/, disclaimer-requirements/, each converted to clean markdown with the argument structure annotated. (3) /citations/ — every TTAB and Federal Circuit case cited in those winning responses, verified to exist, with correct reporter cites and a one-line holding — the anti-hallucination layer. (4) /tmep-extracts/ — the operative TMEP sections per refusal type (TMEP is one free 3,000+page document; the extract-and-map work is the value). (5) /evidence-playbook/ — what exhibits winning responses actually attached (third-party registration printouts, dictionary definitions, marketplace evidence), field by field. (6) /procedure/ — current forms, deadlines, extension fees, response-form field requirements. (7) CHANGELOG.md — dated, updated quarterly.
candidates.source_count: 200+ distinct public records: 150-300 individual TSDR file wrappers (each a separate retrieval: find serial numbers with the refusal type, confirm later registration, download and convert the response PDF), the TMEP, the Trademark ID Manual, USPTO examination guides, and several dozen TTAB/CAFC decisions for the verified-citation layer.
candidates.assembly_effort: 3-4 weeks of directed Claude Code work: scripted TSDR retrieval by status-code sequence, PDF-to-markdown conversion, categorization, and citation verification. Could a competent person with a chat model rebuild it in an afternoon? No — the value is hundreds of retrieved-and-verified public records, not prose. A chat model cannot pull 200 TSDR PDFs, confirm which applications later registered, or verify 100 case citations in an afternoon. The interface file alone could be cloned; the corpus cannot.
candidates.what_ai_gets_wrong_without_it: Fabricated or misattributed case citations — the classic LLM failure in legal drafting (the Mata v. Avianca sanctions line of cases exists precisely because of this) [PLAUSIBLE, widely documented; not re-tested this session]. Also: generic du Pont-factor boilerplate with no evidence exhibits attached (winning responses win on attached evidence, not rhetoric), outdated fees/deadlines (the 3-month deadline replaced 6 months in Dec 2022; USPTO fees changed Jan 2025), and no sense of what examining attorneys actually accept for specimen and ID amendments.
candidates.prompt_test: Best buyer prompt without the folder: 'You are an experienced trademark attorney. Here is my office action [paste]. Draft a complete response to the Section 2(d) refusal with case citations and describe the evidence I should attach.' Honest assessment: this captures maybe 40-50% of the value — the model produces correct structure, the right legal factors, and competent prose. What it cannot supply: citations that are real (they must each be checked), the pattern of exhibits that distinguishes winning responses from arguments, and current procedure/fees. For a simple disclaimer or ID amendment, the free model plus USPTO's page is honestly enough — the product is for substantive refusals, and copy should say so.
candidates.volume_math: USPTO receives roughly 700k+ applications/yr and reported office-action incidence ranges from 25% to 80% depending on measure [PLAUSIBLE — patenttrademarkblog.com, tramatm.com via search; even the lowest estimate implies ~175k office actions/yr]. Target R$30k/mo needs ~$8k/mo = ~55 sales/month at $147 — about 0.03% of annual office-action recipients buying. Below the $197 paid-ads threshold, so this must be organic + marketplace, which the search behavior supports.
candidates.channel: Organic search in the buyer's exact words ('trademark office action response example' is a literal Google autocomplete suggestion), plus Etsy/Gumroad listings where no incumbent exists, plus Reddit/r-Trademark and small-business forums where 'I got an office action, can I respond myself?' threads recur. No audience, no face, no calls — fits Sol.
candidates.demand_evidence: [VERIFIED] Fetched suggestqueries.google.com for 'trademark office action', HTTP 200: suggestions include 'trademark office action response', 'response example', 'response template', 'response extension fee', 'response time' — buyers are literally searching for the product's contents. [VERIFIED] An entire attorney-services ecosystem prices this pain: Trademark Engine at $599+ (fetched).
candidates.free_substitute_check: USPTO itself: I fetched uspto.gov/trademarks/maintain/responding-office-actions (HTTP 200) — it explains deadlines, forms, and general argument principles but provides NO worked examples, no template language, no evidence playbook. Law-firm blogs (Gerben, Erik Pelton) give strategy articles free but never the assembled response set. Nolo covers trademark basics in books but not office-action response corpora. Meegle offers a free 'Office Action Response Generator Template' [PLAUSIBLE, via search — appears to be a generic workflow template on a SaaS, not a response corpus]. The specific asset — organized winning responses with verified citations — is given away by no one.
candidates.saturation_check: [VERIFIED] ActionResponder.ai exists: 'Generate professional responses in minutes... with tailored arguments, real citations, and curated exhibits' — but fetched the site: it is 'Built for Trademark Professionals', attorney testimonials, no public pricing, demo/trial sales motion. It validates the corpus thesis and does not serve the $147 one-shot pro se buyer. Questel (enterprise) and PowerPatent (patents) similar [PLAUSIBLE, via search]. Marketplace check: web search for Etsy office-action templates returned zero Etsy listings; Gumroad discover returned no products for the query (fetched, empty results page). The pro se corpus niche is empty; the attorney SaaS niche is not — watch it.
candidates.regulated_check: Unauthorized practice of law is the adjacent profession; representing others before the USPTO in trademark matters requires a licensed attorney. The line: selling assembled public records and published requirements to a person filing PRO SE is the self-help publisher model (Nolo's) and is lawful; applying law to a specific person's facts is advice. The product never sees the buyer's case — their own AI does the applying (H6 also satisfied). Permitted copy: 'Contains 200 real responses that overcame refusals, retrieved from USPTO public records, organized by refusal type, with every citation verified.' Forbidden copy: 'We'll tell you whether your mark can overcome the refusal' or 'your response should argue...'. Also excluded by rule: foreign-domiciled applicants, who must hire US counsel — state this in the FAQ.
candidates.piracy_answer: Three real mitigations, honestly partial: (1) dated quarterly updates — fees, forms, and the 3-month deadline regime have all changed within 3 years, and product copy sells 'current as of [date]' so a shared stale copy visibly decays; (2) bulk — 200+ files is awkward to re-upload to a forum and impossible to paste into a thread; (3) per-buyer email watermarking in file footers via the delivery platform. Residual risk accepted: one determined buyer can still zip and share; at $147 with a desperate-deadline buyer, most will just buy.
candidates.weakest_link: The honest one: for SIMPLE office actions (disclaimers, ID amendments), free ChatGPT plus USPTO's own page already gets a motivated filer there, so the real market is substantive 2(d)/descriptiveness refusals — a subset — and those buyers may lose anyway even with a good response, creating refund/blame exposure that copy must manage ('improves your draft, does not guarantee registration'). Secondary: ActionResponder or a clone could launch a consumer tier at any time.

[VERIFIED] trademarkengine.com/office-action-response/ fetched HTTP 200 — attorney-assisted response 'starts at $599'. [VERIFIED] actionresponder.ai fetched HTTP 200 — attorney-targeted, no public pricing. [VERIFIED] tsdr.uspto.gov fetched HTTP 200 — free public Status and Documents retrieval per serial number; a live USPTO casedoc URL serving an actual office action document also surfaced in search results (tmng-al.uspto.gov). [VERIFIED] Google autocomplete fetched HTTP 200 — 'response example', 'response template' among suggestions. [PLAUSIBLE] Office-action incidence 25-80% of ~700k+ annual applications (patenttrademarkblog.com, tramatm.com, patentpc.com via search — measures conflict; even the floor supports volume). [PLAUSIBLE] Attorney flat fees $500-2,000+ (multiple firm sites via search). L4SB two-step: $49 evaluation then flat fee (fetched HTTP 200, response prices not disclosed).

candidates.name: FSVP Importer Kit — the Foreign Supplier Verification corpus for US food importers
candidates.one_line: Everything a US food importer's own AI needs to draft and maintain the legally mandatory FSVP file per supplier and food — rule text, FDA's records schema, known-hazard tables by commodity, exemption matrices, and the public record of what FDA cites importers for — before an FDA records request or Import Alert 99-41 stops their shipments.
candidates.buyer: A US business importing food for resale — an Amazon/Shopify grocery or supplement-adjacent seller, an ethnic-foods distributor, a coffee/spice/snack brand importing from its overseas manufacturer. A business with real revenue (each container is $10k-200k+ of goods), reachable in writing, and in 2026 the e-commerce importer segment already runs on ChatGPT. Every one of them is legally an 'FSVP importer' named at entry for every line of food they bring in.
candidates.the_expensive_moment: Three triggers, all searched: (1) their customs broker asks 'who is your FSVP importer?' at first food shipment and they discover a legal duty they've never heard of; (2) FDA emails a records request / schedules an FSVP inspection — 'failure to develop an FSVP' has been FDA's single most-cited food inspection violation since FY2018 [PLAUSIBLE — blog.deibellabs.com FY2023/FY2024 posts and registrarcorp.com via search: 38.4% of all violations, ~44% inspection failure rate, ~1,100-1,900 FSVP inspections/yr]; (3) worst case, the importer lands on Import Alert 99-41's Red List and ALL their food is detained without examination [VERIFIED — fetched accessdata.fda.gov/cms_ia/importalert_1160.html, HTTP 200: named importers on the red list; FDA 'may detain without physical examination an article of human or animal food offered for import by an importer identified on the Red List' under FFDCA 801(a)(3)].
candidates.money_at_stake: Detained or refused shipments are the business's entire inventory pipeline — a single detained container is typically five figures, and red-list removal requires a petition and a clean track record [VERIFIED for the mechanism via the fetched import alert; shipment values PLAUSIBLE]. The paid alternatives price the pain: a human-made FSVP SOP template sells for $499 [VERIFIED — ketki-international.com/product/fsvp-sop-template-service/, fetched HTTP 200], and managed FSVP compliance services (Registrar Corp and similar) run into the thousands per year [PLAUSIBLE — registrarcorp.com service pages via search, prices not published].
candidates.whats_in_the_folder: (1) INSTRUCTIONS.md — how the buyer's AI interviews them about each supplier/food and drafts the FSVP records set from the corpus, information-only framing. candidates.name: Precedent-Grounded Health Insurance Appeal Corpus (external review edition)
candidates.one_line: A folder of ~97,000 real independent-review decisions plus a 50-state external-review rules matrix, so the buyer's own AI drafts an appeal citing how reviewers actually ruled on their exact treatment - instead of inventing precedent.
candidates.buyer: An individual: a US insured patient (or the family member running the fight) whose high-cost treatment - specialty drug, residential mental-health stay, imaging, surgery - was denied as 'not medically necessary', and who is escalating from internal appeal to state external review / IMR. H8: ProPublica and Counterforce Health both document patients already using ChatGPT to appeal denials [PLAUSIBLE - counterforcehealth.org post 'How to Use ChatGPT to Appeal Your Denied Health Insurance Claim' appeared in fetched search results].
candidates.the_expensive_moment: The denial letter arrives (or the internal appeal is denied a second time), the treatment is scheduled or ongoing, and the external-review filing deadline (typically 4 months, some states less) starts running. This is the founder's own floated example, now given the corpus that makes it defensible.
candidates.money_at_stake: The denied treatment itself - specialty drugs and inpatient stays run $10k-100k+/yr. And the fight is winnable: I computed from the actual CA dataset that 22,445 of 42,749 IMR decisions (52.5%) OVERTURNED the health plan [VERIFIED - I downloaded the CSV from data.chhs.ca.gov and computed it]. Penn State reported PA's new external review program overturned about half of 500+ appeals [PLAUSIBLE - porh.psu.edu in search results].
candidates.whats_in_the_folder: (1) master-instructions.md telling the buyer's AI how to locate matching precedents by diagnosis/treatment and draft an appeal grounded only in cited real cases; (2) ca-imr-decisions/ - 42,749 CA DMHC IMR determinations 2001-2026, each with diagnosis category, treatment category, outcome, and full physician-reviewer Findings text, normalized and indexed by treatment [VERIFIED - I downloaded and parsed the CSV]; (3) ny-external-appeals/ - extracts of the 54,051-decision NY DFS public appeal database with per-year Excel exports [VERIFIED - fetched dfs.ny.gov/public-appeal/search HTML showing 'Showing 1 to 10 of 54051']; (4) state-rules-matrix.md - all 50 states' external review deadlines, expedited criteria, fees, and who administers (state vs federal HHS process), assembled from 50 DOI websites; (5) erisa-decision-tree.md - self-funded vs fully-insured routing, since half of employer coverage follows a different path; (6) winning-patterns/ - per-treatment-category digests of what overturning findings actually said (e.g. the 11,948 Pharmacy and 4,835 Mental Health IMR decisions).

candidates.name: Apparel & Footwear Importer's HTS Classification Defense Corpus (CROSS edition)

candidates.buyer: A business: the owner or ops lead of a small US importing brand (DTC apparel, footwear, accessories) importing from Asia - the segment hammered by 2025-26 tariff changes. They have no in-house trade compliance, their broker files whatever HTS they supply, and legal responsibility ('reasonable care', 19 USC 1484) sits with them. H8: e-commerce operators are the most AI-saturated small-business demographic there is.
candidates.the_expensive_moment: A CBP Form 28 'Request for Information' arrives questioning their classification - 30 days to respond, and non-response auto-triggers a Form 29 Notice of Action and rate advances [PLAUSIBLE - consistent across Harris Sliwoski, Torres Trade Law, Rogers & Brown pieces in fetched search results]. Or: this season's tariff math makes a 10-plus-point duty-rate difference between two adjacent codes existential, and they need to know which one survives scrutiny.
candidates.money_at_stake: Apparel duty rates swing roughly 0-32% by code before any Section 301/IEEPA surtaxes, so one wrong code across a year of entries is tens of thousands of dollars; 19 USC 1592 penalties for negligent misclassification run up to 2x the lost duties (4x gross negligence) [PLAUSIBLE - statutory framework, not re-fetched]. A whole broker/law-firm content industry exists around 'what to do when the CF-28 arrives' because the downside is real [VERIFIED that the guides exist - see demand].
candidates.whats_in_the_folder: (1) master-instructions.md - how the buyer's AI walks GRI 1-6 and the chapter notes, finds the closest rulings, checks revocation status, and outputs a classification memo citing ruling numbers; (2) rulings-ch61-62-64/ - the normalized CROSS corpus for knit apparel, woven apparel and footwear: ruling number, date, full text, ruled tariff number(s), revoked/modified flags (the API returns 54,117 hits for 'apparel' and 8,947 for 'footwear'; each ruling's full text is fetchable by number) [VERIFIED - I called rulings.cbp.gov/api/search and /api/ruling/F87174, HTTP 200, got full ruling text with tariff 6110.30.3020]; (3) hts-notes/ - current HTSUS section/chapter notes and stat suffixes for ch. 61/62/64 from USITC; (4) cf28-cf29-playbook.md - response procedure, extension practice, and the published penalty mitigation guidelines (19 CFR Pt. 171 App. B); (5) worked-examples/ - 50 annotated GRI analyses (fiber-content breakpoints, knit-vs-woven, sets, festive exception) each tied to the real rulings that decided it; (6) update-log.md - dated, because rulings and tariff actions change monthly.
candidates.source_count: Five source systems, tens of thousands of documents: the CROSS rulings database (200k+ rulings total; tens of thousands in this niche), the USITC HTSUS, CBP Informed Compliance Publications (~10 relevant, including the apparel guide), Court of International Trade classification opinions, and the CFR mitigation guidelines.
candidates.assembly_effort: 3-4 weeks with Claude Code: the API makes scraping mechanical (search pagination + one call per ruling), but normalizing 60k+ rulings, wiring revocation chains (the API exposes revokedBy/modifies fields - verified), and writing 50 worked GRI examples is real work. candidates.what_ai_gets_wrong_without_it: It hallucinates HTS codes and invents ruling citations - industry sources state plainly that generic LLMs surface the statistically common code rather than reasoning through legal notes, producing confident outputs that fail CBP validation [PLAUSIBLE - gingercontrol.com/Gaia Dynamics pieces in fetched search results; I did not run a live model test].
